{"id": "ac8efcec-2a9a-4b57-8f48-7376dda9b1fd", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "What is the difference between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "56ba0914-491d-4bcf-9e7b-1884754e39a6", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "thinking", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "This is a general AWS concept question rather than something specific to the DevOps Agent product, so I can just answer it directly with well-known information\u2014no need to verify further.\n\n"}]}

{"id": "0d3f52a2-c729-4a54-b4b6-8278f5ad8052", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "The main difference is the network layer each one works at. That determines how each routes traffic and which one fits a given workload.

| | Application Load Balancer (ALB) | Network Load Balancer (NLB) |
|---|---|---|
| **OSI layer** | Layer 7 (application) | Layer 4 (transport) |
| **Protocols** | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, WebSocket | TCP, UDP, TCP_UDP, TLS |
| **Routing** | Content-based. Rules match on path, host header, HTTP headers, query strings, methods, or source IP. | Connection-based. Routes by protocol and port, with flow hashing. |
| **Performance** | Good for web traffic, with slightly higher latency because it inspects requests. | Very high throughput and ultra-low latency. It handles millions of requests per second and sudden traffic spikes. |
| **IP addressing** | Dynamic IPs. You use the DNS name. | One static IP per Availability Zone, and you can attach Elastic IPs. It also supports PrivateLink. |
| **Targets** | Instances, IPs, Lambda functions | Instances, IPs, ALBs |
| **TLS** | Terminates TLS and supports SNI with multiple certificates. It can also authenticate users with Cognito or OIDC. | Supports TLS termination or passthrough. |
| **Client IP** | Passed in the `X-Forwarded-For` header. | Preserved by default for instance targets. |
| **Security groups** | Supported | Supported, but you have to enable them when you create the NLB. |
| **Other features** | Redirects, fixed responses, weighted target groups, WAF integration, and sticky sessions based on cookies. | Supports non-HTTP protocols and long-lived connections. |

**Choose an ALB when:**
- You run HTTP/HTTPS web apps, APIs, or microservices.
- You need path-based or host-based routing, for example `/api` to one service and `/app` to another.
- You want WAF, authentication, or Lambda targets.

**Choose an NLB when:**
- You need extreme performance or very low latency.
- You need static or Elastic IPs, for example for customer firewall allowlists.
- You're load balancing non-HTTP traffic such as gaming, IoT, or custom TCP/UDP protocols.
- You want to expose a service privately through AWS PrivateLink.

You can also chain them. Putting an NLB in front of an ALB gives you static IPs and Layer 7 routing together. If you tell me about your workload, I can suggest which fits better. I can also look at the load balancers in your account.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
